newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia grants awards to Nazi-era war veterans.
newsitem.headline: Croatia grants awards to Nazi-era war veterans.

text.p: Thirteen veteran officers who served with the Croatian forces allied with Nazi Germany during World War Two were awarded equivalent ranks of the country's present-day army, officials said on Monday.
The move was intended to rehabilitate the men, many of whom suffered persecution under communist rule in former Yugoslavia.
It was the latest incident in which state honours were granted to men who fought in Croatia's Nazi-era military units.
The ranks were presented at a conference of the Croatian war veterans' organisation, the Hrvatski Domobran (Croatian Homeguard), in the eastern town of Pozega on Sunday.

Dragutin Franjic, head of veteran's organisation, said the men had served in military units of the Independent State of Croatia (NDH), which broke away from Yugoslavia after the Nazis invaded the Balkans in 1941.
It was a puppet regime of Adolf Hitler's Third Reich and its Ustasha government became notorious for murdering hundreds of thousands of Serbs and Jews during World War Two.

Franjic refused to say whether the officers were members of the Domobrani, the then-regular Croatian conscript army, or the Ustasha militia, a Nazi military formation, responsible for war-time atrocities.
"We only handed over the ranks and the medals," Franjic told Reuters. "It was the President of the Republic (Franjo Tudjman) who awarded them."
Both the defence ministry and the president's military cabinet denied any knowledge of an order to make the awards.

But General Miljenko Crnjac, Tudjman's top military adviser, said a special commission appointed by the defence ministry decides whether war veterans, communist or fascist, qualify for a rank in the modern army that is equivalent to their former rank -- a procedure regulated by Croatian law.
"The President signs the orders for transfer of ranks in groups of 20-30 together, and it is possible that he signed these half a year, or more, ago," Crnjac told Reuters.
Opposition leaders and old communists have often accused Croatia's nationalist government of veiled attempts to whitewash its World War Two record and rehabilitate fascists.
But the government argues that it only wants to reconcile victims of the fighting in World War Two.

Last weekend some 125 bodies of soldiers, including Domobrani, Ustashe and two communist resistance fighters, killed in World War Two, were reburied at a cemetery in the southern town of Omis despite protests from Jewish political groups.
Croatia's 1941-45 collaboration with the Nazis became a political tool for Yugoslav communists who restrained Croatian nationalism inside the Balkan federation for decades.
